question: Next week a charity sells daffodils on your campus to raise money for cancer research. Will you buy at least one?
answer: About 43% bought one. Asked about their classmates, the same students guessed 56%, far nearer the truth than the 83% they forecast for themselves. They knew how people behave; each simply expected to be the exception. The best guide to their own week was the rest of the campus.
move: To predict what you will do, start from what most people do.
ask: Which of my plans would I bet on if a stranger had made them?

options.label: Yes, I'll buy one
options.mirror: Like 83% of the students. In the end 43% bought one: kind plans meet busy weeks.

options.label: No, probably not
options.mirror: Like 17%. A frank forecast: in the end, most of the students didn't buy one either.

scene.why: We forecast ourselves from our intentions, and others from how people act.

reference: Epley & Dunning, Feeling holier than thou: are self-serving assessments produced by errors in self- or social prediction?, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 79 (2000): 861-875
